title: Quince frangipane tart
subtitle: autumn quince poached in spiced syrup on almond frangipane
excerpt: Quince can't be eaten raw, it must be cooked. When poached in a spiced sugar syrup, it turns from pale ivory to a deep rose-gold and develops a floral, perfumed flavour unlike any other fruit. Layered on almond frangipane in a pastry case, quince is at its most dramatic. The pink colour and the honey-like aroma make this an autumn tart worth the extra preparation the quince requires.
sourceNotes: Quince (Cydonia oblonga) was the most widely grown orchard fruit in ancient Greece and Rome and remained prevalent in British kitchen gardens until the 18th century, when softer apple and pear varieties displaced it. It requires long cooking to become palatable and achieves its characteristic pink colour through a reaction between its tannins and the heat during cooking, a colour change well-documented in historical English and French cookery books. The combination of poached quince and frangipane in a tart is a standard of French and Spanish pâtisserie (membrillo, quince paste, is a Spanish speciality). British use of quince in tarts declined as quince trees became rarer, but a revival in garden quince growing from the 1990s onward has brought it back into domestic baking.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Poach the quince the day before; the colour deepens overnight. Bake the tart on the day.
recipe.temperatureNote: for baking the frangipane; blind bake at 190°C first

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: 180°C conventional (160°C fan) for the frangipane; 190°C for the blind bake

content.text: Quince frangipane tart requires poaching the quince first, raw quince is rock-hard and bitter. The poaching takes about an hour over low heat; the reward is the dramatic colour change and the extraordinary fragrance. Lay the poached quince on top of the frangipane and bake until the almond cream puffs up around it.

Peel, quarter, and core the quince (they are hard, use a heavy knife). Cut each quarter in half lengthways. Dissolve the sugar in the water in a large saucepan over a medium heat. Add the vanilla pod, cinnamon stick, and quince pieces. Bring to a gentle simmer, cover with a cartouche (a piece of parchment cut to the pan size, laid on the surface), and poach on a low heat for 50 to 60 minutes. The quince is ready when it has turned pale rose-gold to deep pink and a knife goes through without resistance. Leave the quince to cool in the syrup.
Blind bake and fill the tart

Make and blind bake the pastry case at 190°C in the usual way. Preheat the oven to 180°C conventional (160°C fan). Beat the butter and sugar for the frangipane until pale. Add the eggs one at a time, then fold in the ground almonds. Spread the frangipane in the pastry case. Lift the poached quince pieces from the syrup and arrange over the frangipane, pressing them in gently. Bake for 35 to 40 minutes until the frangipane is set and lightly golden. Brush the warm tart with a little of the reduced poaching syrup to glaze.
